compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional school event, either person might step in when a teacher is absent. That choice could follow from their role, prior experience or a request for help. It does not establish any of the shared letters.

The three shared letters each mean something separate. E turns attention and energy toward what is happening outside; N notices connection, pattern and possibility when gathering material; J forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward. Read as three statements, not one, they stop "likes organising" from being treated as the sum of the letters — being able to gather people may come from responsibility, or from having been pushed into it.

The split is T against F: which kind of basis judgement rests on more often. One side asks whether the rule can be applied consistently, and whether responsibility and cost can be accounted for; the other asks what this means for specific people, and whether the relationship can still hold. Both sides can use both kinds of basis; the difference is which one more often takes the deciding seat.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: one equipment failure, two ways of weighing the fix

In a fictional school sports day, the equipment goes to the wrong venue twenty minutes before the first event. After the team recovers the equipment, both organizers consider the same proposal: add a second sign-off to the equipment checkout form next year, even though it adds time to each pickup.

A Feeling consideration is how the extra sign-off would affect the volunteers and whether it could feel like an accusation. Either organizer could raise that concern and still support the procedure if the team explains its purpose.

A Thinking consideration is whether the same sign-off rule could apply to all pickups and whether the delay it adds is proportionate to the risk of another mix-up. Either organizer could raise that concern and still consider how to explain the rule to volunteers.

Both trade-offs carry a cost, and both are conditional. Explanation alone risks the same failure recurring, harder to explain the second time; a checkpoint without explanation risks people feeling watched, and fewer volunteers for the equipment team next year. Which cost weighs more depends on the size of the team, how often equipment changes hands, and whether something similar has happened before.

The team can check the location on the dispatch note, how long recovery took and whether a later mix-up was recorded. Tone or the number of chat messages does not establish whether someone prefers Thinking or Feeling.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: why the two common stacks differ only in the first and fourth seats

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The difference is not a function moving seats but which judging process occupies the same seat: Fe against Te in the first position, Ti against Fi in the fourth. The second and third positions are Ni and Se for both in this writing, unchanged.

This arrangement describes which standard judgement leans on more; it does not say the two gather information the same way, and it does not say who should own which step. Sharing Ni and Se is only a shared name inside the model; nothing follows about the two seeing a problem equally fast or equally accurately, and still less about allocating tasks.

Whether the third process should be marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform: some tables give only the function name, others always assign Se. When a different version turns up, check which one it states; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone acts. Item-by-item preferences sit on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Two people running the same event should not divide the work into one soft and one hard. What works is putting the requirements of the post, each person's experience and their willingness on the table, then seeing how the two bases of judgement fit together; type does not enter the division of work.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: after the sports day, who apologises and who rewrites the process

In this fictional aftermath both face the same issue sheet and the same people. One can invite the person affected to explain how the rework affected them, then establish which team owns the responsibility; the other can bring the traceable records and set out the dispatch, the recovery and the standard for next time's signature. Both bases can go into one retrospective, and who carries which material has nothing to do with personality.

Each approach has a gap: human warmth alone lets the hole repeat; process alone may leave nobody willing to take the equipment team next year. The steadier approach does both and only decides who speaks at the front. Which side someone is more practised at depends on how many times they have done it and whether anyone taught them, not on letters.

Two-colour marking works, but for finding gaps rather than counting proportions. Print the draft retrospective and mark one colour for who was affected and who communicated, another for which step failed and what checkpoint gets added; look for a whole section missing one colour. The missing half usually needs someone to cover it, and how much each colour occupies has nothing to do with type.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: the parents' group changes the date — ask everyone, or post one notice

(Fictional scene) The sports day moves to next week because of heavy rain, and four parents have already taken leave. One consideration puts the emphasis on each of those four situations — one used annual leave, one has to bring a child — and tends toward asking each privately before sending a single notice; the other puts the emphasis on a consistent, workable message and tends toward writing the new time, the refund and change options and the forms to be refilled into one pinned post, handling individual cases from the list. Either consideration can come from the same person, and the order of approaches shifts with conditions.

Each has a cost: asking individually can travel slowly, a single notice can leave those four feeling overlooked. An agreement can set the notice out within ten minutes and individual follow-ups within two hours; that is a process agreement, not a basis for typing. Who does which part depends on who is free and who knows the parents better.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: splitting the extra cost after a reunion dinner

(Fictional scene) A ten-year reunion ends with a bill above the prepaid amount: the room charge, drinks, and two family members brought along at short notice. One approach attends more to who barely ate, who came with a child, who has just changed jobs, and is willing to cover the difference personally and collect privately according to face; the other attends more to whether headcount, drinks and room charge can be split into three columns and worked out, and tends to read the calculation aloud in the group so that whoever paid less tops up. Either approach can be taken by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

Each has a cost: money covered personally may partly never come back and will be read as willingness; reciting the calculation settles the bill but may leave the person who brought family exposed. Counterexamples are common: an ENTJ may quietly waive the share of whoever is short, and an ENFJ may work the bill out to the last digit.

To check how the split actually went, look at the payment records and what the people involved said afterwards: who topped up how much, who commented later. The number of replies in the group and the length of private chats cannot be used to infer motive, still less to decide anyone's type.

compare_blocks.body:
Thinking does not measure warmth, and Feeling does not measure willingness to enforce a rule. Either person might check on a volunteer privately or ask for an incomplete equipment form to be corrected.

The second misread comes from position: whoever sits at the head of the table and speaks in imperatives may simply have been put there; conversely, a soft-spoken person may make the call at the critical moment.

The third mismatch writes the difference as a ranking of ability. Clear allocation of responsibility is not the same as strong management, and attending to people is not the same as strong coordination; both can be trained, and both fail under fatigue.

The fourth uses the order of actions as a test. "He steadied people first, so he is F" ignores that the same person behaves in a completely different order when time is short, when facing strangers, or when the other party is a superior. Order can describe this once; it cannot define the person.

body: In a fictional school event, either person might step in when a teacher is absent. That choice could follow from their role, prior experience or a request for help. It does not establish any of the shared letters.

The three shared letters each mean something separate. E turns attention and energy toward what is happening outside; N notices connection, pattern and possibility when gathering material; J forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward. Read as three statements, not one, they stop "likes organising" from being treated as the sum of the letters — being able to gather people may come from responsibility, or from having been pushed into it.

The split is T against F: which kind of basis judgement rests on more often. One side asks whether the rule can be applied consistently, and whether responsibility and cost can be accounted for; the other asks what this means for specific people, and whether the relationship can still hold. Both sides can use both kinds of basis; the difference is which one more often takes the deciding seat.
### ENFJ and ENTJ: one equipment failure, two ways of weighing the fix

In a fictional school sports day, the equipment goes to the wrong venue twenty minutes before the first event. After the team recovers the equipment, both organizers consider the same proposal: add a second sign-off to the equipment checkout form next year, even though it adds time to each pickup.

A Feeling consideration is how the extra sign-off would affect the volunteers and whether it could feel like an accusation. Either organizer could raise that concern and still support the procedure if the team explains its purpose.

A Thinking consideration is whether the same sign-off rule could apply to all pickups and whether the delay it adds is proportionate to the risk of another mix-up. Either organizer could raise that concern and still consider how to explain the rule to volunteers.

Both trade-offs carry a cost, and both are conditional. Explanation alone risks the same failure recurring, harder to explain the second time; a checkpoint without explanation risks people feeling watched, and fewer volunteers for the equipment team next year. Which cost weighs more depends on the size of the team, how often equipment changes hands, and whether something similar has happened before.

The team can check the location on the dispatch note, how long recovery took and whether a later mix-up was recorded. Tone or the number of chat messages does not establish whether someone prefers Thinking or Feeling.
### ENFJ and ENTJ: why the two common stacks differ only in the first and fourth seats

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The difference is not a function moving seats but which judging process occupies the same seat: Fe against Te in the first position, Ti against Fi in the fourth. The second and third positions are Ni and Se for both in this writing, unchanged.

This arrangement describes which standard judgement leans on more; it does not say the two gather information the same way, and it does not say who should own which step. Sharing Ni and Se is only a shared name inside the model; nothing follows about the two seeing a problem equally fast or equally accurately, and still less about allocating tasks.

Whether the third process should be marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform: some tables give only the function name, others always assign Se. When a different version turns up, check which one it states; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone acts. Item-by-item preferences sit on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).

body: Two people running the same event should not divide the work into one soft and one hard. What works is putting the requirements of the post, each person's experience and their willingness on the table, then seeing how the two bases of judgement fit together; type does not enter the division of work.
### ENFJ and ENTJ: after the sports day, who apologises and who rewrites the process

In this fictional aftermath both face the same issue sheet and the same people. One can invite the person affected to explain how the rework affected them, then establish which team owns the responsibility; the other can bring the traceable records and set out the dispatch, the recovery and the standard for next time's signature. Both bases can go into one retrospective, and who carries which material has nothing to do with personality.

Each approach has a gap: human warmth alone lets the hole repeat; process alone may leave nobody willing to take the equipment team next year. The steadier approach does both and only decides who speaks at the front. Which side someone is more practised at depends on how many times they have done it and whether anyone taught them, not on letters.

Two-colour marking works, but for finding gaps rather than counting proportions. Print the draft retrospective and mark one colour for who was affected and who communicated, another for which step failed and what checkpoint gets added; look for a whole section missing one colour. The missing half usually needs someone to cover it, and how much each colour occupies has nothing to do with type.
### ENFJ and ENTJ: the parents' group changes the date — ask everyone, or post one notice

(Fictional scene) The sports day moves to next week because of heavy rain, and four parents have already taken leave. One consideration puts the emphasis on each of those four situations — one used annual leave, one has to bring a child — and tends toward asking each privately before sending a single notice; the other puts the emphasis on a consistent, workable message and tends toward writing the new time, the refund and change options and the forms to be refilled into one pinned post, handling individual cases from the list. Either consideration can come from the same person, and the order of approaches shifts with conditions.

Each has a cost: asking individually can travel slowly, a single notice can leave those four feeling overlooked. An agreement can set the notice out within ten minutes and individual follow-ups within two hours; that is a process agreement, not a basis for typing. Who does which part depends on who is free and who knows the parents better.
### ENFJ and ENTJ: splitting the extra cost after a reunion dinner

(Fictional scene) A ten-year reunion ends with a bill above the prepaid amount: the room charge, drinks, and two family members brought along at short notice. One approach attends more to who barely ate, who came with a child, who has just changed jobs, and is willing to cover the difference personally and collect privately according to face; the other attends more to whether headcount, drinks and room charge can be split into three columns and worked out, and tends to read the calculation aloud in the group so that whoever paid less tops up. Either approach can be taken by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

Each has a cost: money covered personally may partly never come back and will be read as willingness; reciting the calculation settles the bill but may leave the person who brought family exposed. Counterexamples are common: an ENTJ may quietly waive the share of whoever is short, and an ENFJ may work the bill out to the last digit.

To check how the split actually went, look at the payment records and what the people involved said afterwards: who topped up how much, who commented later. The number of replies in the group and the length of private chats cannot be used to infer motive, still less to decide anyone's type.

body: Thinking does not measure warmth, and Feeling does not measure willingness to enforce a rule. Either person might check on a volunteer privately or ask for an incomplete equipment form to be corrected.

The second misread comes from position: whoever sits at the head of the table and speaks in imperatives may simply have been put there; conversely, a soft-spoken person may make the call at the critical moment.

The third mismatch writes the difference as a ranking of ability. Clear allocation of responsibility is not the same as strong management, and attending to people is not the same as strong coordination; both can be trained, and both fail under fatigue.

The fourth uses the order of actions as a test. "He steadied people first, so he is F" ignores that the same person behaves in a completely different order when time is short, when facing strangers, or when the other party is a superior. Order can describe this once; it cannot define the person.

body: When two results differ, check the item set first: the same questions, the same version, the same language, and which part of life you had in mind while answering. The term spent finishing a thesis and the term just after starting may draw on two different selves.

A useful practice is to record trade-offs rather than count them. After each decision where someone has to bear the consequences, write down the alternatives considered, the cost of each, the reason finally adopted, and the constraints of your role at the time — who was present, who was responsible, how tight the deadline was. There is no need to score the two sides or count which kind of reason appears more.

If the two results still disagree, keeping the uncertainty is acceptable. Take the notes and compare them with the base descriptions on both sides to see which sits closer to the reasons you gave across several situations; that is self-understanding, not typing, and it does not replace checking the assessment tool itself.

Emphasis inside the model is not behaviour, and it does not say who should lead a team or who is better at looking after people. Facing the same equipment failure, either type may fetch replacements, steady the people and reconstruct the timeline; the difference shows up more often in which kind of reason gets cited when a trade-off has to be made.
sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional school event, either person might step in when a teacher is absent. That choice could follow from their role, prior experience or a request for help. It does not establish any of the shared letters.

The three shared letters each mean something separate. E turns attention and energy toward what is happening outside; N notices connection, pattern and possibility when gathering material; J forms an arrangement and a conclusion outward. Read as three statements, not one, they stop "likes organising" from being treated as the sum of the letters — being able to gather people may come from responsibility, or from having been pushed into it.

The split is T against F: which kind of basis judgement rests on more often. One side asks whether the rule can be applied consistently, and whether responsibility and cost can be accounted for; the other asks what this means for specific people, and whether the relationship can still hold. Both sides can use both kinds of basis; the difference is which one more often takes the deciding seat.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: one equipment failure, two ways of weighing the fix

In a fictional school sports day, the equipment goes to the wrong venue twenty minutes before the first event. After the team recovers the equipment, both organizers consider the same proposal: add a second sign-off to the equipment checkout form next year, even though it adds time to each pickup.

A Feeling consideration is how the extra sign-off would affect the volunteers and whether it could feel like an accusation. Either organizer could raise that concern and still support the procedure if the team explains its purpose.

A Thinking consideration is whether the same sign-off rule could apply to all pickups and whether the delay it adds is proportionate to the risk of another mix-up. Either organizer could raise that concern and still consider how to explain the rule to volunteers.

Both trade-offs carry a cost, and both are conditional. Explanation alone risks the same failure recurring, harder to explain the second time; a checkpoint without explanation risks people feeling watched, and fewer volunteers for the equipment team next year. Which cost weighs more depends on the size of the team, how often equipment changes hands, and whether something similar has happened before.

The team can check the location on the dispatch note, how long recovery took and whether a later mix-up was recorded. Tone or the number of chat messages does not establish whether someone prefers Thinking or Feeling.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: why the two common stacks differ only in the first and fourth seats

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and ENTJ is Te–Ni–Se–Fi. The difference is not a function moving seats but which judging process occupies the same seat: Fe against Te in the first position, Ti against Fi in the fourth. The second and third positions are Ni and Se for both in this writing, unchanged.

This arrangement describes which standard judgement leans on more; it does not say the two gather information the same way, and it does not say who should own which step. Sharing Ni and Se is only a shared name inside the model; nothing follows about the two seeing a problem equally fast or equally accurately, and still less about allocating tasks.

Whether the third process should be marked introverted or extraverted is not uniform: some tables give only the function name, others always assign Se. When a different version turns up, check which one it states; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone acts. Item-by-item preferences sit on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [ENTJ profile](/en/personality/entj).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions first: the same day, the same batch of equipment, the same issue sheet, the same deadline. Both types can use both columns; the rows describe evidence that may get more attention in a trade-off, not who is faster or stronger. These two types differ only on T/F, so all six rows land on the standard of judgement, simply looking at different sides of it; the last column says so.

| The same decision point (same day, same equipment, same deadline) | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | ENTJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether the issue sheet gets a countersignature | Who the procedure lands on, and whether the person asked to sign feels suspected | The cost of a repeat failure, and whether responsibility can be fixed to a step | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F: cost of trust against cost of recurrence |
| Whether the post-event note names the person who missed the venue | Weigh how including the name would affect the person and the team, within the same reporting rules | Apply the same traceability and privacy requirements to every incident report | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F: someone's position against traceability |
| Both decide what to include in the same incident report | Weigh which verified details would help affected people understand what happened | Apply the same relevance and evidence criteria used for other incident reports | Decision criteria: T/F |
| Both prepare the same briefing for the sports department | Weigh how the wording would affect the people involved while keeping the verified timeline intact | Apply the same criteria for what an incident briefing must document and what follow-up it must assign | Decision criteria: T/F |
| Both choose a coordinator under the same role requirements | Consider how the assignment would affect each volunteer and the support available to them | Apply the same availability, experience and accountability criteria to each volunteer | Decision criteria: T/F. Both approaches still use the role requirements. |
| Being asked on the spot whether to add a helper | Whether adding someone makes the current team feel distrusted | Whether the extra hand closes the gap, and whether the cost is bearable | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F: felt trust against gap and cost |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An ENFJ who has run the equipment team for three years may put the countersignature straight into the sheet; an ENTJ taking it over for the first time may only want the wording to land well. With twenty minutes left, either may skip the discussion and fetch the equipment. Role, experience, deadline and how many people are present all rewrite the approach, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.
sections.title: ENFJ and ENTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Two people running the same event should not divide the work into one soft and one hard. What works is putting the requirements of the post, each person's experience and their willingness on the table, then seeing how the two bases of judgement fit together; type does not enter the division of work.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: after the sports day, who apologises and who rewrites the process

In this fictional aftermath both face the same issue sheet and the same people. One can invite the person affected to explain how the rework affected them, then establish which team owns the responsibility; the other can bring the traceable records and set out the dispatch, the recovery and the standard for next time's signature. Both bases can go into one retrospective, and who carries which material has nothing to do with personality.

Each approach has a gap: human warmth alone lets the hole repeat; process alone may leave nobody willing to take the equipment team next year. The steadier approach does both and only decides who speaks at the front. Which side someone is more practised at depends on how many times they have done it and whether anyone taught them, not on letters.

Two-colour marking works, but for finding gaps rather than counting proportions. Print the draft retrospective and mark one colour for who was affected and who communicated, another for which step failed and what checkpoint gets added; look for a whole section missing one colour. The missing half usually needs someone to cover it, and how much each colour occupies has nothing to do with type.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: the parents' group changes the date — ask everyone, or post one notice

(Fictional scene) The sports day moves to next week because of heavy rain, and four parents have already taken leave. One consideration puts the emphasis on each of those four situations — one used annual leave, one has to bring a child — and tends toward asking each privately before sending a single notice; the other puts the emphasis on a consistent, workable message and tends toward writing the new time, the refund and change options and the forms to be refilled into one pinned post, handling individual cases from the list. Either consideration can come from the same person, and the order of approaches shifts with conditions.

Each has a cost: asking individually can travel slowly, a single notice can leave those four feeling overlooked. An agreement can set the notice out within ten minutes and individual follow-ups within two hours; that is a process agreement, not a basis for typing. Who does which part depends on who is free and who knows the parents better.

### ENFJ and ENTJ: splitting the extra cost after a reunion dinner

(Fictional scene) A ten-year reunion ends with a bill above the prepaid amount: the room charge, drinks, and two family members brought along at short notice. One approach attends more to who barely ate, who came with a child, who has just changed jobs, and is willing to cover the difference personally and collect privately according to face; the other attends more to whether headcount, drinks and room charge can be split into three columns and worked out, and tends to read the calculation aloud in the group so that whoever paid less tops up. Either approach can be taken by the same person, and the order depends on the task and the information available.

Each has a cost: money covered personally may partly never come back and will be read as willingness; reciting the calculation settles the bill but may leave the person who brought family exposed. Counterexamples are common: an ENTJ may quietly waive the share of whoever is short, and an ENFJ may work the bill out to the last digit.

To check how the split actually went, look at the payment records and what the people involved said afterwards: who topped up how much, who commented later. The number of replies in the group and the length of private chats cannot be used to infer motive, still less to decide anyone's type.
sections.title: ENFJ and ENTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Thinking does not measure warmth, and Feeling does not measure willingness to enforce a rule. Either person might check on a volunteer privately or ask for an incomplete equipment form to be corrected.

The second misread comes from position: whoever sits at the head of the table and speaks in imperatives may simply have been put there; conversely, a soft-spoken person may make the call at the critical moment.

The third mismatch writes the difference as a ranking of ability. Clear allocation of responsibility is not the same as strong management, and attending to people is not the same as strong coordination; both can be trained, and both fail under fatigue.

The fourth uses the order of actions as a test. "He steadied people first, so he is F" ignores that the same person behaves in a completely different order when time is short, when facing strangers, or when the other party is a superior. Order can describe this once; it cannot define the person.
sections.title: ENFJ and ENTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the item set first: the same questions, the same version, the same language, and which part of life you had in mind while answering. The term spent finishing a thesis and the term just after starting may draw on two different selves.

A useful practice is to record trade-offs rather than count them. After each decision where someone has to bear the consequences, write down the alternatives considered, the cost of each, the reason finally adopted, and the constraints of your role at the time — who was present, who was responsible, how tight the deadline was. There is no need to score the two sides or count which kind of reason appears more.

If the two results still disagree, keeping the uncertainty is acceptable. Take the notes and compare them with the base descriptions on both sides to see which sits closer to the reasons you gave across several situations; that is self-understanding, not typing, and it does not replace checking the assessment tool itself.
sections.title: ENFJ and ENTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
You cannot, from one action. Both ENFJ and ENTJ steady people, and both trace responsibility; the difference is which basis gets cited in a trade-off.

In the fictional equipment mix-up, either organizer might weigh how a second sign-off would affect volunteers and whether the same rule could be applied consistently. Those are two ways to talk about decision criteria. A single action or stated reason cannot establish a type.
items.question: If I can watch only one action, how do I tell them apart?

items.answer:
Not two functions changing seats, but a different judging process in the same seat: Fe against Te in the first position, Ti against Fi in the fourth. In the common writing used here, Ni in second and Se in third are the same on both sides.

The arrangement describes only which standard judgement leans on more; it does not say the two gather information the same way, and it does not say who suits which step. Whether the third process gets an attitude marking is handled differently across tables; the writing here is an editorial convention and not the Foundation's only reading.
items.question: They differ by one letter — why do the stacks change only two positions?

items.answer:
They are distinct, but not by whether the behaviour exists, and not by who does it first. Looking after people and setting rules are learnable behaviours; T/F describes which basis more often holds the deciding seat when there is a choice.

Look back over several similar matters: when explaining a decision, do you more often cite "this rule is the same for everyone, and cost and responsibility can be accounted for", or "this puts someone in a difficult position, and the relationship may not survive it". The same person uses both; one phrasing, or behaviour when tired, cannot settle it.
items.question: An ENTJ also looks after people, an ENFJ also sets rules — how are they still distinct?

items.answer:
Either can do it. The work has four parts — communication, scheduling, resources and closing — and doing it well depends on the requirements of the role, prior experience and personal willingness, none of which maps onto four letters.

A workable approach writes one sentence for each part about which you would willingly do repeatedly, then compares that with the real job description and what you have actually done. Divide by who is good at what and who has time, not by type; if both want the same part, split it into the outward-facing and internal halves.
items.question: Which is better suited to running a class event?

items.answer:
In this kind of event preparation, two things are worth preventing: a commitment already made outside being changed unilaterally, and a person being treated as the problem itself. These are not the pair's most likely failures in general, only common friction points in the scene on this page.

A workable agreement works in layers: one side owns the single outward channel, the other chairs the internal retrospective; the retrospective discusses steps only, and anything about a person moves to a private conversation. In a dispute, ask whether what is changing is the promise or the method — a method can be settled on the spot, a promise needs to be communicated outward first.
items.question: Where do they most often get stuck when working together?

items.answer:
Align the item sets first: the same questions, the same version, the same language, and which experience you were referring to. If they still disagree, keeping the uncertainty is acceptable; there is no need to award it to the higher score or the more frequent result.

Ask which situations you had in mind and how much room you had to choose. If the same questionnaire reports a T/F score and explains its cutoff, read the score in that context. Notes from comparable decisions can help you reflect, but they do not establish which result is more accurate.
